briefs.learning_objective: Understand a company's mission and values well enough to filter product decisions against them.

required_facts.statement: A mission states the present purpose of an organization and whom it serves.
Values express the principles that guide how an organization pursues its purpose.
A product direction should fit the organization’s mission and values.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Draft a mission by identifying the organization’s purpose, audience, and value, then check a proposed product direction against that purpose.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/mission-and-vision :: How to Write a Mission Statement: Purpose, Examples, & Templates

briefs.learning_objective: Articulate a concise, aspirational statement of the future state the product aims to create for its customers and business.

required_facts.statement: Product vision describes the future state a product is intended to achieve and the value it will provide.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Vision gives a shared direction for decisions rather than a list of detailed implementation tasks.
Draft a vision by stating the product’s purpose, the customers it serves, and the desired future impact.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Review a draft vision with the team and target users to refine whether it is clear and motivating.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: A vision should not be rewritten for every small change in the product’s underlying plan.

briefs.learning_objective: Articulate the specific value a product delivers to a defined customer segment.

required_facts.statement: A value proposition communicates the benefit a product delivers to a specific target customer.
The message should address the customer’s problem or job and explain the benefit or gain the product creates.
Write a proposition by naming the target customer, the problem relieved, and the distinct benefit provided.
Check that the value is expressed in terms the customer can understand rather than a list of product features.

misconceptions.statement: A value proposition is not just a slogan or promotional tagline.

briefs.learning_objective: Systematically assess competitor products/strategies to identify gaps and threats relevant to a product decision.

required_facts.statement: Competitive analysis examines alternatives customers could choose, including indirect competitors.
A structured comparison can include features, pricing, market position, strengths, and weaknesses.
Identify the relevant competitors and compare them using the same dimensions.
Use gaps, weaknesses, and differences in the comparison to identify an opportunity or threat relevant to the product.

briefs.learning_objective: Define where a product sits relative to competitors and alternatives in the customer's mind.

required_facts.statement: Product positioning describes how a product is presented to its intended market relative to alternatives.
A positioning statement identifies the target customer, the need, the product category, the principal benefit, and the reason to believe the differentiation.
Write positioning by completing those elements and checking whether it emphasizes customer benefits instead of merely listing features.

misconceptions.statement: Positioning is not a fixed message that should remain unchanged when the market changes.

briefs.learning_objective: Connect a product decision or roadmap item explicitly to a stated business goal.

required_facts.statement: Product goals describe outcomes the product should achieve, not just activities a team will carry out.
Business goals describe the benefit the product should deliver to the organization.
Connect product initiatives to measurable goals that support the organization’s direction.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Specify a goal’s intended result, measurement, and time boundary so progress can be assessed.

misconceptions.statement: A product decision can create local progress while conflicting with a higher-level strategy.

briefs.learning_objective: Plan and conduct one-on-one qualitative interviews to surface unmet customer needs and pain points.

required_facts.statement: Customer interviews gather qualitative accounts of needs, experiences, and problems through guided conversation.
Start an interview plan with a research goal and recruit people whose experience is relevant to it.
Build a discussion guide with open-ended, neutral prompts about concrete past experiences.
During the conversation, listen and ask follow-up questions to clarify what happened, why it mattered, and how the person responded.

misconceptions.statement: An interview reports what a person says; it does not directly establish what they do while using an interface.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply the Jobs-to-Be-Done framework to reframe a customer problem in terms of the job the customer is 'hiring' a product to do.

required_facts.statement: Jobs to Be Done examines the outcome a customer wants to achieve rather than starting from a feature.
A customer job is a task or problem the person is trying to resolve, with functional, emotional, or social dimensions.
Identify a job by investigating the customer’s situation, obstacles, desired outcome, and existing way of getting the task done.
Frame an opportunity around the desired outcome and compare current alternatives by how well they help achieve it.
Write a job statement with the triggering situation, the customer’s motivation, and the outcome they want rather than a requested feature.

briefs.learning_objective: Synthesize raw, unstructured customer feedback (support tickets, reviews, calls) into recurring themes.

required_facts.statement: Voice of Customer captures feedback about customers’ experiences, needs, and preferences.
Feedback can come from interviews, surveys, reviews, and customer-facing teams.
Collect feedback across channels and look for recurring needs and pain points rather than treating each request as a separate instruction.
Use the recurring themes to identify opportunities that address customer problems.
Group related observations into themes and record recurrence and the user consequence associated with each theme.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/affinity-diagram/ :: Affinity Diagramming for Sorting UX Findings and Ideas - NN/G

misconceptions.statement: A single feedback channel may omit important customer perspectives.

briefs.learning_objective: Design a quantitative survey instrument that measures a specific research question without introducing bias.

required_facts.statement: Survey design starts with the research question and the information needed to answer it.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/?lm=should-you-run-a-survey&pt=article :: Writing Good Survey Questions: 10 Best Practices - NN/G

required_facts.statement: Closed-ended questions provide predefined response options for quantitative summaries.
Open-ended questions allow respondents to describe their answer in their own words.
Write questions in neutral, clear language and choose response options that are mutually exclusive and collectively cover plausible answers.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/?lm=should-you-run-a-survey&pt=article :: Answer Options Should Be All-Inclusive and Mutually Exclusive

required_facts.statement: Pilot a survey before distributing it to check whether people interpret the questions and options as intended.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/?lm=should-you-run-a-survey&pt=article :: Writing Good Survey Questions: 10 Best Practices - NN/G

required_facts.statement: Ask about one issue per question so a respondent is not forced to give a single answer to two different questions.

misconceptions.statement: Respondents’ predictions of their future behavior are unreliable evidence of what they will actually do.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/survey-best-practices/?lm=should-you-run-a-survey&pt=article :: Don’t Ask Respondents to Predict Behavior

briefs.learning_objective: Divide a market into meaningful segments based on shared needs or characteristics.

required_facts.statement: User groups can be distinguished by shared behaviors, goals, needs, and pain points.
Segments help specify which users a product direction is intended to serve.
Derive useful groups by looking for recurring similarities and differences in research about user behavior and needs.
Define a proposed segment’s common need and relevant characteristics, then check it against the intended audience and product direction.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-strategy :: What is a Product Strategy? [+How to Build One] | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Demographic similarity alone need not imply similar user goals or behaviors.

briefs.learning_objective: Estimate the total, serviceable, and obtainable market size for a product opportunity.

required_facts.statement: Total Addressable Market estimates the total potential market opportunity for a product or service.
A top-down estimate narrows a broad market using external industry data and relevant constraints.
A bottom-up estimate uses the number of potential customers and annual revenue per customer to estimate annual market revenue.
Document the assumptions behind the customer count and revenue estimate so the opportunity estimate can be checked.

briefs.learning_objective: Synthesize research findings into a representative customer persona that guides product decisions.

required_facts.statement: A user persona represents a recurring type of user grounded in research about needs and behavior.
A persona should communicate relevant goals, behaviors, motivations, and pain points.
Draft a persona by consolidating research patterns and recording the user’s goal, activities, and problem context.
Use the persona to examine whether a proposed product decision addresses that user type’s needs.

misconceptions.statement: Adding a plausible name or photograph does not replace research into user needs.
source_refs: nngroup_articles#https://www.nngroup.com/articles/personas-archetypes/ :: Personas Put a Single Face to Many Users

briefs.learning_objective: Plan and moderate a usability test session to observe how a user actually completes a task with a design/prototype.

required_facts.statement: A usability test observes representative users attempting tasks with a product or prototype.
A basic usability test involves a participant, task, and facilitator.
Select realistic tasks and participants relevant to the product’s intended use.
Observe where participants succeed or struggle and record the evidence without directing them toward the answer.
Summarize observed obstacles into findings that can guide improvements.

misconceptions.statement: Usability testing is not the same as asking people whether they like an interface.

briefs.learning_objective: Recognize and evaluate the signals that indicate a product satisfies strong market demand.

required_facts.statement: Product-market fit means a product meets a significant market need and customers are willing to use or pay for it.
Qualitative customer feedback and quantitative indicators can contribute evidence of product-market fit.
Gather evidence of demand and customer value from willingness to pay, satisfaction, and recommendations.
Assess fit from a combination of evidence rather than declaring it from one isolated response.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a clear, evidence-backed statement of the customer/business problem being addressed.

required_facts.statement: A problem statement identifies the affected user, the problem, and its consequence without prescribing a solution.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Evidence of the problem should connect it to an observable cost such as wasted time, money, or dissatisfaction.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Write a problem statement by naming who encounters the problem, what happens, and why it matters.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Check that a draft focuses on the user problem rather than a favored feature.

briefs.learning_objective: Reframe a problem statement and generate a range of candidate solution directions before committing to one, using 'How Might We' framing.

required_facts.statement: How Might We questions turn research problems or insights into prompts for solution exploration.
A useful prompt is broad enough to admit multiple approaches but specific enough to focus on the identified problem.
Write a prompt as “How might we” followed by the desired user outcome, without naming a particular solution.
Prefer positive outcome language that makes the desired change clear.
Generate alternative ideas without judging them during the initial brainstorming phase.

briefs.learning_objective: Specify a proposed solution's behavior in enough detail for engineering and design to build it.

required_facts.statement: A solution specification describes the proposed behavior and boundaries of the product change.
The specification links the proposal to the user problem, goals, functional behavior, and constraints.
Write the proposal by explaining the approach, expected behavior, included scope, exclusions, and key constraints.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-specification :: How to write a product specification

required_facts.statement: Review it with engineering and design to resolve ambiguity before implementation.

briefs.learning_objective: Keep the problem being solved distinct from the solution chosen to solve it throughout a spec.

required_facts.statement: A problem statement describes the user need or difficulty; a solution statement describes a proposed way of addressing it.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Combining the two too early can hide assumptions and narrow the alternatives the team considers.
Rewrite a muddled statement into a problem describing who is affected and why, followed by a separate proposal describing the chosen behavior.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Check that the proposed solution addresses the stated problem without redefining the problem as the absence of that solution.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a PRD that documents what will be built and why, sufficient for engineering to start work.

required_facts.statement: A product specification describes what is to be built and the requirements it must satisfy.
A PRD captures a product’s purpose, features, behavior, and release requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/requirements :: What is a product requirements document (PRD)?

required_facts.statement: Construct a specification with purpose, user needs, functional and nonfunctional requirements, scope, and constraints.
Review the specification with engineering and design to clarify ambiguity and missing requirements.

misconceptions.statement: A specification should evolve when new information changes the requirements; it is not necessarily a one-time handoff.

briefs.learning_objective: Summarize an initiative's problem, solution, and impact on a single page for broad audiences.

required_facts.statement: A product brief is a short document for aligning the team around an idea before detailed delivery work.
Its core content is the problem, intended audience, goals, success metrics, scope, assumptions, and open questions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: How to write a product brief

required_facts.statement: Draft the brief by clarifying the problem and audience before describing the proposed approach.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 2: Clarify the problem and audience

required_facts.statement: Share the brief for feedback and revise it until the team understands the purpose and boundaries of the work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 6: Share, revise, and connect the brief to delivery work

required_facts.statement: For a requested one-page summary, keep the problem, proposed solution, intended impact, and essential context while removing specialist detail.

briefs.learning_objective: Write user stories in the standard format capturing who, what, and why for a unit of work.

required_facts.statement: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective.
The common story form is “As a [user], I want [capability], so that [benefit].”
Write a story by naming the user, the goal or capability, and the reason it matters.
Discuss stories with the team and split large work into smaller stories that communicate distinct user value.

misconceptions.statement: A user story is not a complete detailed technical specification.

briefs.learning_objective: Define the testable conditions that must be true for a story to be considered done.

required_facts.statement: Acceptance criteria state the observable conditions a particular work item must satisfy to be accepted.
Criteria should be clear and testable so the team can determine whether a condition is met.
Write criteria around the intended behavior and relevant constraints rather than vague judgments.
Use the criteria to compare the delivered behavior with the agreed requirements.

misconceptions.statement: Acceptance criteria should describe the required outcome without unnecessarily dictating its implementation.

briefs.learning_objective: Diagram the sequence of steps a user takes to complete a task within a product.

required_facts.statement: A user flow maps the steps a user takes to accomplish a task within a product.
A flow identifies entry points, actions or screens, decisions, and possible endpoints.
Sketch a flow by naming the user’s task, mapping the steps and decision branches, and marking completion or failure endpoints.
Review the flow for missing steps and unnecessary friction between the entry point and the user’s goal.

briefs.learning_objective: Define the metrics that will determine whether a feature or initiative succeeded.

required_facts.statement: A success metric quantifies whether the intended product outcome is being achieved.
A useful target links a specific metric to a measurable, achievable result and time boundary.
Choose metrics that match the goal of the proposed change rather than simply collecting available counts.
Record the current benchmark, desired target, and period for judging whether the change succeeded.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a roadmap that communicates the sequenced direction of a product over time.

required_facts.statement: A product roadmap communicates product direction, priorities, and progress over time.
Roadmap content and level of detail should be chosen for its audience.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

required_facts.statement: Translate product goals into prioritized initiatives and place them on an understandable planning horizon.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

required_facts.statement: Update the roadmap often enough to remain a trustworthy source of direction and progress.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: Best practices for the best roadmaps

misconceptions.statement: A roadmap should not be overloaded with all detailed delivery tasks.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: Best practices for the best roadmaps

briefs.learning_objective: Estimate how much roadmap work a team can realistically take on given its available capacity.

required_facts.statement: Capacity planning estimates the work a team can realistically take on with its available people and time.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

required_facts.statement: Recent completed work can inform the forecast, but availability and external constraints can change future capacity.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

required_facts.statement: Check planned work against availability, holidays, dependencies, and known risks before committing to a timeframe.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

required_facts.statement: Adjust scope or timing when planned work exceeds the capacity available.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

required_facts.statement: Calculate historical velocity as completed work units divided by the number of observed iterations; a baseline period forecast is average velocity × available iterations, adjusted for changed availability.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

misconceptions.statement: Adding people does not guarantee a proportional increase in completed work because coordination overhead can rise.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: Factors that can affect Scrum velocity

briefs.learning_objective: Sequence roadmap themes into concrete release cycles.

required_facts.statement: Release planning assigns selected roadmap work to upcoming release windows.
A release plan is more tactical and detailed than the roadmap’s directional view.
Group work into release windows by considering goals, priority, scope, capacity, and dependencies.
Check that prerequisite work comes early enough to enable dependent items and revise the windows if the schedule is infeasible.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to manage dependencies in project management

briefs.learning_objective: Order features/work within a plan based on dependency, value, and risk.

required_facts.statement: Feature sequencing places already-prioritized features in an executable order.
A feature that requires another feature’s output cannot be scheduled as if it were independent.
List prerequisites and dependency relationships, then order the features so prerequisites are available when needed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to identify dependencies in a project

required_facts.statement: Use the existing relative priorities to choose among feasible sequences and explain any dependency-driven change in order.

briefs.learning_objective: Estimate calendar delivery dates for roadmap items given team capacity and scope.

required_facts.statement: A delivery forecast connects estimated work with the team’s recent completion rate and available time.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

required_facts.statement: With consistently estimated work, estimated iterations equal remaining work units divided by historical average units completed per iteration.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

required_facts.statement: Convert the iteration estimate into a date range using iteration length, current timing, and plausible variation in completion rate.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

required_facts.statement: State the forecast’s assumptions about scope, team availability, dependencies, and historical variability.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: Factors that can affect Scrum velocity

misconceptions.statement: A historical average is a forecast input, not a guarantee of the same future rate.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/velocity-scrum :: How to calculate velocity in Scrum

briefs.learning_objective: Set a coherent set of priorities and goals for a single quarter that ladder up to the roadmap.

required_facts.statement: A quarterly roadmap organizes product direction and intended progress across three-month planning periods.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: Product Roadmap Guide: What is it & How to Create One | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Quarterly goals should connect to longer-term objectives while remaining measurable within the quarter.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

required_facts.statement: Map selected initiatives to goals, assign owners, and identify milestones for the quarter.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

required_facts.statement: Check timelines against team capacity and dependencies before communicating the quarterly plan.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

required_facts.statement: Review progress and changing conditions to adjust subsequent quarterly priorities.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/quarterly-planning :: A Guide to Quarterly Planning: Key Components, Tips, & Templates

briefs.learning_objective: Scope a multi-sprint initiative (a program-level body of work) with a clear goal and success criteria.

required_facts.statement: An initiative is a body of work intended to advance a specific product or business goal.
An initiative brief makes the problem, audience, goal, scope, assumptions, and success criteria explicit.
Start from the strategic theme and describe the outcome the initiative is meant to achieve.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: What Is a Product Brief? How to Write One & Example

required_facts.statement: Write the included scope, exclusions, and measures that would demonstrate the intended outcome.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: Step 4: Outline scope, assumptions, and open questions

briefs.learning_objective: Identify and manage cross-team dependencies that affect roadmap-level sequencing.

required_facts.statement: A dependency exists when one piece of work needs output or information from another.
Dependency relationships determine whether tasks can start or finish independently or must be sequenced.
Map dependencies by identifying the provider, needed output, dependent task, and required handoff point.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to identify dependencies in a project

required_facts.statement: Review dependencies with the involved teams and communicate changes that could delay downstream work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to manage dependencies in project management

misconceptions.statement: Dependencies can cross teams and business functions rather than existing only within one team.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to identify dependencies in a project

briefs.learning_objective: Define the minimum set of functionality needed to test a product hypothesis with real users.

required_facts.statement: An MVP is a limited product version built to learn whether a product idea meets customer needs with less initial investment.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/minimum-viable-product :: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?

required_facts.statement: The scope must retain enough of the core value for the intended users to try it and provide useful feedback.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/minimum-viable-product :: What Is a Minimum Viable Product?

required_facts.statement: Define the target user and learning goal, then select only the capabilities needed to deliver and test the core value.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/minimum-viable-product :: What Is a Minimum Viable Product?

required_facts.statement: List excluded enhancements and explain why they are unnecessary for the initial value and learning goal.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/minimum-viable-product :: What Is a Minimum Viable Product?

misconceptions.statement: An MVP is not simply an arbitrary incomplete product with the maximum number of features removed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/minimum-viable-product :: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?

briefs.learning_objective: Plot initiatives on a value-vs-effort 2x2 to identify quick wins and time sinks.

required_facts.statement: An impact-effort matrix compares initiatives on two dimensions: expected value or importance and implementation effort.
The four quadrants are high-impact/low-effort, high-impact/high-effort, low-impact/low-effort, and low-impact/high-effort.
Define a common interpretation of impact and effort and plot each initiative in the corresponding quadrant.
Use high-impact/low-effort items as strong early candidates and examine the tradeoff for high-impact/high-effort items.

briefs.learning_objective: Judge the likely magnitude of effect an initiative will have on a target outcome before committing resources.

required_facts.statement: Impact assessment estimates how much a proposed initiative would contribute to a target outcome.
Choose a common target metric and impact scale before comparing initiatives.
Estimate the expected contribution using research or observed product evidence, then explain the assumptions behind it.
State confidence separately so a promising but speculative effect is not treated as equally reliable as an evidence-backed estimate.

briefs.learning_objective: Score and rank initiatives using Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort.

required_facts.statement: RICE compares initiatives using reach, impact, confidence, and effort.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/rice-scoring-model :: What is the RICE Scoring Model for Prioritization?

required_facts.statement: Reach is the estimated number of affected people or occurrences in a specified timeframe.
Impact estimates the contribution per affected person or occurrence to the chosen goal.
Confidence expresses how well evidence supports the estimates and is used as a proportional factor.
Effort estimates the total work required using a consistent unit such as person-months.
Calculate RICE as reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort and compare scores using consistent assumptions and scales.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: Why is ICE Scoring Useful and Who Created it?

misconceptions.statement: A RICE score is not proof that uncertain impact estimates are accurate.

briefs.learning_objective: Score and rank initiatives using Impact, Confidence, and Ease for fast, low-data prioritization.

required_facts.statement: ICE compares ideas using impact, confidence, and ease.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: What is the ICE Scoring Model?

required_facts.statement: Impact estimates the expected effect on the target goal.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: What is the ICE Scoring Model?

required_facts.statement: Confidence rates the certainty that the predicted effect will occur.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: What is the ICE Scoring Model?

required_facts.statement: Ease rates how straightforward the work is to complete, with higher ease favoring less difficult work.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: What is the ICE Scoring Model?

required_facts.statement: Using the ProductPlan convention, rate each factor from 1 to 10, multiply impact × confidence × ease, and rank higher scores first.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: What is the ICE Scoring Model?

misconceptions.statement: ICE scores are subjective unless the team agrees on what each scale value means.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/ice-scoring-model :: Why is ICE Scoring Useful and Who Created it?

briefs.learning_objective: Rank initiatives using a custom weighted set of criteria relevant to the product context.

required_facts.statement: Weighted scoring ranks options by combining ratings across criteria with explicit relative importance weights.
Criteria should reflect the current strategic benefits and costs relevant to the decision.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How can product managers use weighted scoring?

required_facts.statement: Set criteria, define a consistent scoring scale, and assign weights before evaluating the options.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How can product managers use weighted scoring?

required_facts.statement: Calculate each option’s total by multiplying each criterion score by its weight and summing the weighted contributions.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How do you calculate weighted scoring?

required_facts.statement: Compare totals while checking how changes in priorities or assumptions would affect the ranking.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How do you analyze weighted scoring results?

misconceptions.statement: Numerical scores do not remove disagreements about the assumptions used to create them.

briefs.learning_objective: Explicitly weigh competing options against each other when a prioritization framework alone doesn't resolve a decision.

required_facts.statement: A tradeoff is a choice in which obtaining one benefit can require accepting a cost or giving up another benefit.
Compare alternatives against the same goals, benefits, costs, and constraints.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How can product managers use weighted scoring?

required_facts.statement: Write the advantages and disadvantages of each option and make the opportunity cost of choosing one explicit.
Recommend the option that best fits the stated priorities and explain the downside being accepted.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/weighted-scoring :: How do you analyze weighted scoring results?

briefs.learning_objective: Classify features by the type of customer satisfaction they produce (basic, performance, delighter).

required_facts.statement: Kano classifies features according to how their presence or absence affects customer satisfaction.
Basic features are expected and can create dissatisfaction when missing or inadequate.
Performance features increase satisfaction as their performance improves.
Delighters can create disproportionate satisfaction when present even though customers may not miss them when absent.
Indifferent features attract little customer interest, while dissatisfaction features can upset customers.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/kano-model :: What are the Kano Model Feature Categories?

required_facts.statement: Classify candidate features using customer feedback and consider the investment needed to provide an appropriate mix.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/kano-model :: How Does the Kano Model Work?

briefs.learning_objective: Communicate roadmap priorities using coarse time horizons instead of fixed dates.

required_facts.statement: A Now-Next-Later roadmap groups work into current, upcoming, and more distant priorities instead of relying on exact delivery dates.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Now describes work currently in focus.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Next describes the work expected to follow the current priorities.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Later holds longer-term ideas whose details and timing are less certain.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Place initiatives into the three buckets according to priority and readiness, then revisit the buckets as information changes.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

misconceptions.statement: Next and Later are not promises of fixed completion dates.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/learn/blog-customer-feature-requests :: How to Handle Customer Feature Requests Without Overpromising | ProductPlan

briefs.learning_objective: Classify requirements by Must/Should/Could/Won't to scope a single release.

required_facts.statement: MoSCoW sorts work into Must-have, Should-have, Could-have, and Won’t-have-for-now categories.
Must-haves are non-negotiable requirements for the specified release or timebox.
Should-haves are important but can be deferred without making the current release unusable.
Could-haves are desirable additions whose omission has less effect than omitting a Should-have.
Won’t-have-for-now items are explicitly outside the current timebox but may be considered later.
Agree on the timebox, goals, and category meanings, then classify each requirement by the consequence of leaving it out.

misconceptions.statement: MoSCoW labels do not supply an objective ranking among all items within the same category.

briefs.learning_objective: Identify stakeholders and manage their expectations and influence over a product initiative.

required_facts.statement: Stakeholder analysis identifies people affected by a product decision and examines their needs and influence.
A power-interest map distinguishes high-power/high-interest, high-power/low-interest, low-power/high-interest, and low-power/low-interest stakeholders.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/stakeholder-analysis :: How do You Conduct a Stakeholder Analysis?

required_facts.statement: Manage high-power/high-interest stakeholders closely and keep high-power/low-interest stakeholders satisfied.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/stakeholder-analysis :: How do You Conduct a Stakeholder Analysis?

required_facts.statement: Keep low-power/high-interest stakeholders informed and monitor low-power/low-interest stakeholders with proportionate effort.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/stakeholder-analysis :: How do You Conduct a Stakeholder Analysis?

required_facts.statement: Create a stakeholder map by listing stakeholders, assessing their power and interest, and choosing the corresponding engagement approach.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/stakeholder-analysis :: How do You Conduct a Stakeholder Analysis?

required_facts.statement: Use stakeholder analysis to decide whom to engage and tailor the frequency and content of communication.

briefs.learning_objective: Work effectively with functions outside product (eng, design, sales, support) toward a shared outcome.

required_facts.statement: Cross-functional collaboration brings different specialties together around a shared outcome.
A shared goal, clear roles, and open communication help coordinate work across functions.
Map the needed contributions, assign owners, and identify handoffs and shared milestones.
Agree on communication channels and review points so issues are surfaced across team boundaries.
For cross-functional friction, make each function’s needs and constraints explicit and seek an option that supports the shared outcome.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

misconceptions.statement: Putting people from different functions in one meeting does not by itself establish a shared way of working.

briefs.learning_objective: Bring a group with differing opinions to a shared, workable decision.

required_facts.statement: Consensus building involves developing shared understanding and working toward an agreement people can support.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/unanimity-based-product-decisions/ :: Making Unanimous Product Decisions | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Unanimity requires active support from everyone involved; consent requires no meaningful unresolved objection.
Choose and state the decision rule before the discussion so participants understand how agreement will be established.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/decision-rules-to-make-better-product-decisions/ :: Use Decision Rules to Make Better Product Decisions | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Invite concerns, investigate their reasons, and revise the proposal or compare alternatives to seek an acceptable agreement.
If consensus is impractical, agree on an alternative decision rule explicitly and document the decision and remaining objections.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/decision-rules-to-make-better-product-decisions/ :: Use Decision Rules to Make Better Product Decisions | Roman Pichler

misconceptions.statement: Silence or pressure-induced agreement is not reliable evidence of consent.

briefs.learning_objective: Adapt the content and framing of a message to fit a specific audience's needs and context.

required_facts.statement: Audience adaptation changes emphasis, terminology, and detail to suit the recipient’s needs.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-collaboration/communication-plan :: How to create a communication plan

required_facts.statement: Different audiences need different information from the same product update.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

required_facts.statement: Identify what each audience needs to understand or decide, then tailor the message’s content and language accordingly.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-collaboration/communication-plan :: How to create a communication plan

required_facts.statement: Keep the underlying facts consistent while varying detail and tone for each audience.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-collaboration/communication-plan :: How to create a communication plan

briefs.learning_objective: Communicate initiative progress accurately and concisely to relevant audiences on a regular cadence.

required_facts.statement: A status report summarizes current progress, obstacles, risks, and next steps for a defined audience.
Compare actual progress with the intended plan and identify significant deviations.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/status-report :: Project Status Report: Tips and Templates for Success | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Write the update with completed progress, current status, important risks or blockers, and next actions with owners.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/status-report :: Project Status Report: Tips and Templates for Success | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Make any needed decision or help request explicit and keep the update concise enough for its audience.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/status-report :: Project Status Report: Tips and Templates for Success | Atlassian

briefs.learning_objective: Communicate to executives/leadership concisely, leading with the decision or ask.

required_facts.statement: Executive communication emphasizes the information leadership needs for direction or a decision.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

required_facts.statement: Summarize detailed work in terms of business outcomes, progress, and consequential risks.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/status-report :: Project Status Report: Tips and Templates for Success | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Lead with the headline, state the decision or support needed, and name the key risk or implication.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/status-report :: Project Status Report: Tips and Templates for Success | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Keep technical detail subordinate to the executive’s immediate information need.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

briefs.learning_objective: Craft messaging that communicates a product's value in language the target audience understands.

required_facts.statement: Product messaging communicates the product’s value to its intended audience.
A clear headline should foreground the customer benefit rather than an unexplained feature label.
Write a headline and supporting points that connect the customer problem to the benefit and meaningful differentiation.
Check that the language and claims match the chosen audience and positioning.

briefs.learning_objective: Present a roadmap to a given audience in a way that sets accurate expectations.

required_facts.statement: Effective roadmap communication explains the product direction and the reasons behind priorities.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/tips-for-presenting-product-roadmaps :: 10 Tips to Nail a Product Roadmap Presentation | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: The audience determines the appropriate level of detail and emphasis.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: How to create a product roadmap

required_facts.statement: Prepare an update that connects priorities and progress to product goals, flags changes, and states what input is needed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/tips-for-presenting-product-roadmaps :: 10 Tips to Nail a Product Roadmap Presentation | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Provide a clear way for stakeholders to ask questions and access the current roadmap.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/tips-for-presenting-product-roadmaps :: 10 Tips to Nail a Product Roadmap Presentation | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Providing excessive roadmap detail can make the message harder to understand rather than more useful.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-roadmaps :: Best practices for the best roadmaps

briefs.learning_objective: Resolve a disagreement between stakeholders in a way that keeps the initiative moving.

required_facts.statement: Conflict resolution identifies and addresses the competing needs beneath disagreement.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Listen to each participant’s perspective and separate observable events from blame or interpretation.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Restate the shared goal and underlying needs, then generate alternatives that could address them.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/how-to-leverage-conflict-in-product-management/ :: How to Leverage Conflict in Product Management

required_facts.statement: Agree on a workable option and state the tradeoff, accepted downside, and follow-up action.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

briefs.learning_objective: Negotiate priorities or scope with a stakeholder who has different goals, often without formal authority.

required_facts.statement: Negotiation seeks a workable agreement between people with differing needs or concerns.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: A stated position is what someone asks for; the underlying need explains why it matters.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Ask about the other party’s concerns, explain your own needs, and look for options that can address both.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

required_facts.statement: Compare alternatives and tradeoffs against shared goals rather than treating the conversation as a contest to win.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/how-to-leverage-conflict-in-product-management/ :: How to Leverage Conflict in Product Management

misconceptions.statement: A forced compromise can leave the underlying conflict unresolved.
source_refs: pichler_blog#https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/conflict-resolution-tips-product-managers-product-owners/ :: Dealing with Difficult Stakeholders and Team Members | Roman Pichler

briefs.learning_objective: Own and maintain a prioritized, well-groomed backlog that reflects current priorities.

required_facts.statement: The product backlog is an ordered, evolving list of work needed to improve the product.
The Product Owner is accountable for ordering backlog items and making the backlog visible and understood.
Review a messy backlog against the product goal, remove obsolete items, clarify relevant work, and place the most valuable upcoming items first.
Explain the top items’ value and ordering, and revisit the order as customer or business needs change.

misconceptions.statement: A backlog is not a fixed promise to implement every item ever added to it.

briefs.learning_objective: Facilitate relative sizing of backlog items so a team can plan sprint capacity.

required_facts.statement: Estimation expresses the anticipated effort, complexity, and uncertainty of work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/estimation :: What are story points in Agile and how do you estimate them? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Story points are relative units rather than a universal conversion into hours.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/estimation :: What are story points in Agile and how do you estimate them? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Compare a work item with previously understood items and discuss differences in effort, risk, and complexity.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/estimation :: What are story points in Agile and how do you estimate them? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Planning poker has team members select estimates independently, reveal them, discuss differences, and re-estimate toward agreement.
Use estimates to inform scope and planning, then review them against experience to improve future estimates.

misconceptions.statement: Story points should not be treated as a measure of an individual’s productivity.

briefs.learning_objective: Hold a PM-depth conversation with engineering to sanity-check a proposed solution's feasibility before committing it to a roadmap.

required_facts.statement: Technical feasibility assesses whether a proposed solution can be built with the available technology, skills, and constraints.
A PM supplies the intended user outcome and product constraints while engineering evaluates technical options and limitations.
Ask engineering about implementation constraints, dependencies, technical uncertainty, and the effort needed to achieve the proposed behavior.
Clarify whether an answer identifies a hard constraint, a manageable risk, or a cost-and-scope tradeoff, then adjust the proposal accordingly.

misconceptions.statement: A PM-depth feasibility discussion is not a substitute for engineering’s implementation design.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html :: Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?

briefs.learning_objective: Understand what a PM/PO contributes to Sprint Planning: presenting priority and clarifying acceptance criteria for candidate backlog items.

required_facts.statement: Sprint Planning creates the upcoming sprint’s plan through collaboration across the Scrum Team.
The Product Owner prepares the important backlog items and explains how they map to the Product Goal.
The team establishes a Sprint Goal, while Developers select feasible work using their past performance and upcoming capacity.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html :: Topic Two: What can be Done this Sprint?

required_facts.statement: Prepare a PM/PO briefing with the proposed goal, priority rationale, clear item scope, and answers to value or requirement questions.

misconceptions.statement: The PM/PO does not dictate how Developers turn selected backlog items into working product increments.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html :: Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?

briefs.learning_objective: Understand the PM/PO's role in a Daily Scrum: listening for blockers and scope risk without turning it into a status meeting.

required_facts.statement: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the upcoming plan.
A Product Owner participates as a Developer when actively working on sprint backlog items; it is not inherently a management status meeting.
Identify impediments or unresolved product questions from the discussion and clarify who needs to act on them.
Handle detailed follow-up outside the short event and involve the appropriate owner instead of interrupting team self-management.

briefs.learning_objective: Understand the PM/PO's role in a Sprint Review: demoing completed work to stakeholders and gathering feedback against the goal.

required_facts.statement: A sprint review inspects completed product work with stakeholders and gathers feedback about next steps.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/sprint-reviews :: What is a Sprint Review in Agile? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: The review considers completed and incomplete work in relation to the sprint goal and product direction.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/sprint-reviews :: What is a Sprint Review in Agile? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Prepare a review agenda with the goal, demonstrations of completed work, stakeholder questions, and feedback capture.
Use feedback and changed circumstances to reconsider upcoming priorities and clarify next steps.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/sprint-reviews :: What is a Sprint Review in Agile? | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: A sprint review is distinct from a retrospective, which examines the team’s working process.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/scrum/sprint-reviews :: What is a Sprint Review in Agile? | Atlassian

briefs.learning_objective: Understand the PM/PO's role in a Sprint Retrospective: contributing to process improvement without dominating the discussion.

required_facts.statement: A sprint retrospective inspects how the team worked and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness.
The Scrum Team examines interactions, processes, tools, problems, and assumptions and chooses useful improvements.
Triage actions about product goals, backlog clarity, or backlog ordering to the Product Owner’s accountability.
Leave technical work planning with Developers and process improvements as collaborative team work rather than automatically assigning every action to the PM/PO.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html :: Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?

required_facts.statement: Assign clear follow-up ownership for the chosen improvements and address high-impact changes promptly.

briefs.learning_objective: Prepare upcoming backlog items (clarify, size, split) so they're ready for a future sprint.

required_facts.statement: Backlog refinement is ongoing review and clarification of upcoming work so the team can plan and execute it.
Refinement can include clarifying requirements, splitting large items, estimating effort, and reconsidering order.
Review an item for a clear user outcome, understood scope, acceptance conditions, dependencies, and manageable size.
Work with the team to resolve gaps, split oversized items, and update estimates and ordering as appropriate.

misconceptions.statement: Refinement is not limited to a single mandatory meeting held once before execution.

briefs.learning_objective: Balance technical debt paydown against feature work in prioritization decisions.

required_facts.statement: Technical debt is the future cost or reduced flexibility created by development choices that defer technical work.
Debt can be taken deliberately or arise inadvertently, and its consequences can accumulate over time.
Identify a debt item by describing the deferred work, its current impact, and the likely cost of leaving it unresolved.
Discuss repayment with the team and weigh it against other work using the impact on future delivery and product quality.
Reserve an explicit share of available capacity for debt work when its impact justifies it, and explain the resulting feature-versus-debt tradeoff rather than assuming a universal ratio.

misconceptions.statement: Technical debt is not inherently a bad decision; some tradeoffs can be reasonable under real constraints.

briefs.learning_objective: Identify and track blocking dependencies between teams at the sprint level.

required_facts.statement: A sprint-level blocker is a dependency that prevents selected work from progressing toward the Sprint Goal.
Identify the needed output, its provider, the blocked item, and the handoff date.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to identify dependencies in a project

required_facts.statement: Confirm the provider’s status and coordinate a workaround, alternative sequence, or escalation with the involved teams.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/project-management-dependencies :: How to manage dependencies in project management

required_facts.statement: Keep the blocker and agreed action visible until the dependency is resolved.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards :: What is a kanban board? | Atlassian

briefs.learning_objective: Manage a Kanban board's flow and WIP limits to keep work moving smoothly.

required_facts.statement: Workflow states describe the stages a work item passes through from entry to completion.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards :: What is a kanban board? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Cards represent individual work items and columns make their current stages visible.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards :: What is a kanban board? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: A WIP limit sets the maximum number of items allowed in a workflow stage.
When a stage reaches its limit, help finish or unblock existing items rather than starting additional work in that stage.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards :: What is a kanban board? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Review bottlenecks and adjust limits based on observed flow rather than assuming the initial limits are permanent.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/wip-limits :: Working with WIP limits for kanban | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Higher limits are not automatically better; excess parallel work can lengthen delivery time.

briefs.learning_objective: Define and apply the shared checklist that determines when a piece of work is truly complete.

required_facts.statement: Definition of Done is the team’s shared set of conditions for considering work complete and ready for customers.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the definition of done?

required_facts.statement: The conditions should be specific enough for the team to check completion and quality consistently.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile? | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Create the definition collaboratively with the people responsible for delivering and using the work.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: Work with the right team members

required_facts.statement: Apply the shared checklist to an increment before treating it as complete, and resolve any unmet conditions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile? | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Definition of Done is not identical to the item-specific conditions that describe whether a particular requirement was implemented correctly.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/project-management/definition-of-done :: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Agile? | Atlassian

briefs.learning_objective: Coordinate the steps needed to safely ship a set of completed work to production.

required_facts.statement: A release plan is a tactical document that captures and tracks features intended for an upcoming release.
Release planning connects agreed scope to delivery timing and responsibilities.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-release :: Product release guide: Key phases and best practices | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Prepare the plan by defining release goals and scope, sequencing work, and identifying dependencies and readiness tasks.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-release :: Product release guide: Key phases and best practices | Atlassian

required_facts.statement: Include post-release monitoring and support so unexpected user problems can be identified and addressed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-release :: Product release guide: Key phases and best practices | Atlassian

misconceptions.statement: Technical availability and a market-facing launch are distinct and need not be the same event.

briefs.learning_objective: Identify the single metric that best captures the core value a product delivers to customers.

required_facts.statement: A North Star metric captures a central measure of the value customers receive from a product.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

required_facts.statement: A useful North Star metric reflects customer value, is within the team’s influence, and is connected to sustained business results.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

required_facts.statement: Choose a candidate by identifying the product’s core customer value and the observable behavior that indicates receipt of that value.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

required_facts.statement: Identify contributing input metrics that teams can act on to improve the central value measure.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

misconceptions.statement: Revenue alone may not represent whether customers are receiving the product’s core value.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/product-north-star-metric :: Every Product Needs a North Star Metric: Here’s How to Find Yours

briefs.learning_objective: Set an ambitious objective paired with measurable key results using the OKR format.

required_facts.statement: An OKR pairs an objective describing a desired direction with key results that measure its achievement.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/objectives-and-key-results :: Objectives and Key Results | Glossary | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: The objective is qualitative and motivating; key results are measurable outcomes with clear targets.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/objectives-and-key-results :: Objectives and Key Results | Glossary | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Write an OKR by stating the intended improvement and a small set of measurable results that would demonstrate it.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/objectives-and-key-results :: Objectives and Key Results | Glossary | ProductPlan

required_facts.statement: Review progress against the key-result targets during the agreed planning period.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/objectives-and-key-results :: Objectives and Key Results | Glossary | ProductPlan

misconceptions.statement: Completing a list of activities does not by itself demonstrate achievement of a key result.
source_refs: productplan_glossary#https://www.productplan.com/glossary/objectives-and-key-results :: Objectives and Key Results | Glossary | ProductPlan

briefs.learning_objective: Distinguish leading indicators (predictive, early) from lagging indicators (outcome, late) when choosing what to monitor.

required_facts.statement: A leading indicator tracks a precursor that can help predict a later outcome.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/leading-lagging-indicators :: Leading vs. Lagging Indicators (With Real-World Examples)

required_facts.statement: A lagging indicator measures an outcome after it has occurred.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/leading-lagging-indicators :: Leading vs. Lagging Indicators (With Real-World Examples)

required_facts.statement: Classify a metric by asking whether it measures an input or precursor to the target outcome or the realized outcome itself.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/leading-lagging-indicators :: Leading vs. Lagging Indicators (With Real-World Examples)

required_facts.statement: Use leading indicators to guide timely action and lagging indicators to check whether the intended result followed.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/leading-lagging-indicators :: Leading vs. Lagging Indicators (With Real-World Examples)

misconceptions.statement: A leading indicator is not a guarantee of the later outcome.

briefs.learning_objective: Formulate and validate a falsifiable hypothesis before running an experiment.

required_facts.statement: A hypothesis states an expectation that can be evaluated using evidence.
A testable product hypothesis links a specific proposed change to an expected outcome for a defined audience.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: What Is a Product Brief? How to Write One & Example

required_facts.statement: Write the hypothesis by specifying the change, expected metric direction, affected audience, and conditions for judging the result.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management/product-brief :: What Is a Product Brief? How to Write One & Example

required_facts.statement: Check that the expectation can be contradicted by an observable result rather than merely expressing an aspiration.
Set the smallest result that would count as success and identify evidence that would contradict the expectation before testing it.

briefs.learning_objective: Read a product analytics dashboard and draw correct conclusions from it.

required_facts.statement: A product analytics dashboard brings together measures that support monitoring product performance.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/dashboard-reporting :: What is Dashboard Reporting? A Guide to Data-Driven Insights

required_facts.statement: Interpret a chart in the context of its metric definition, time window, audience, and benchmark or target.
Look for changes in trend or unusual values and compare related measures before drawing a conclusion.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/dashboard-reporting :: What is Dashboard Reporting? A Guide to Data-Driven Insights

required_facts.statement: State the observed anomaly separately from a plausible explanation and identify what further evidence would test that explanation.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/data-driven-data-informed-data-inspired :: Are You Data-driven, Data-informed or Data-inspired?

misconceptions.statement: A dashboard correlation alone does not establish why a metric changed.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/data-driven-data-informed-data-inspired :: Are You Data-driven, Data-informed or Data-inspired?

briefs.learning_objective: Define what events and properties need to be tracked to measure a feature's success before it ships.

required_facts.statement: An event records a user action or occurrence in a product, and event properties describe its context.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/explore/data/event-taxonomy :: What Is Event Taxonomy: Complete Definition & Framework

required_facts.statement: A tracking plan defines the events and properties to collect so product questions can be answered consistently.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/create-tracking-plan :: How To Create a Tracking Plan? - The Definitive Guide

required_facts.statement: Start a tracking plan with the questions to answer, then list only the key events needed to answer them.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/create-tracking-plan :: How To Create a Tracking Plan? - The Definitive Guide

required_facts.statement: For each event, specify its name, when it occurs, source, owner, and relevant properties with types and expected values.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/create-tracking-plan :: How To Create a Tracking Plan? - The Definitive Guide

required_facts.statement: Use consistent naming and review the plan with implementation partners before collecting the data.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/explore/data/event-taxonomy :: What Is Event Taxonomy: Complete Definition & Framework

misconceptions.statement: Tracking every click can create unnecessary data and implementation work rather than better understanding.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://amplitude.com/blog/create-tracking-plan :: How To Create a Tracking Plan? - The Definitive Guide

briefs.learning_objective: Analyze a multi-step conversion funnel to find where users drop off.

required_facts.statement: A funnel is an ordered sequence of actions leading toward a target outcome.
Conversion is completion of the target step; drop-off is the loss of users between steps.
Define the steps and timeframe, then compare the number of users reaching each step.
Calculate a step’s conversion as users reaching the next step divided by users at the previous step, and use the difference to locate drop-off.
Investigate the stages with substantial drop-off to identify friction rather than assuming the counts explain its cause.

briefs.learning_objective: Compare groups of users by shared start date/attribute to understand retention over time.

required_facts.statement: A cohort is a group of users who share a defined characteristic or behavior.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/customer-cohort-analysis-vs-user-cohort-analysis :: Customer Cohort Analysis vs User Cohort Analysis: What’s The Difference?

required_facts.statement: Retention analysis follows whether members of a defined cohort return or remain active over time.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/customer-cohort-analysis-vs-user-cohort-analysis :: Customer Cohort Analysis vs User Cohort Analysis: What’s The Difference?

required_facts.statement: Define the cohort entry condition and the action that counts as a return, then observe later periods relative to entry.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/customer-cohort-analysis-vs-user-cohort-analysis :: Customer Cohort Analysis vs User Cohort Analysis: What’s The Difference?

required_facts.statement: Compare retention across cohorts or periods to see whether continued use is improving or declining.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/customer-cohort-analysis-vs-user-cohort-analysis :: Customer Cohort Analysis vs User Cohort Analysis: What’s The Difference?

misconceptions.statement: An overall customer count can obscure differences between newly acquired users and established users.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://blog.amplitude.com/customer-cohort-analysis-vs-user-cohort-analysis :: Customer Cohort Analysis vs User Cohort Analysis: What’s The Difference?

briefs.learning_objective: Design and interpret an A/B test to measure the causal effect of a single change.

required_facts.statement: A/B testing compares a control experience with a changed version to assess a predefined outcome.
Random assignment helps make the comparison less dependent on preexisting differences between user groups.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://help.amplitude.com/hc/en-us/articles/115001580108-Analyze-A-B-test-results-in-Amplitude :: Analyze A/B test results in Amplitude | Amplitude Docs

required_facts.statement: Define a hypothesis, primary metric, target audience, and planned run conditions before exposing users to the variants.
Compare the variants on the chosen metric and evaluate statistical uncertainty before concluding that the change improved the outcome.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://help.amplitude.com/docs/en/feature-experiment/workflow/experiment-learnings :: Learn from your experiment | Amplitude Docs

required_facts.statement: Duration feasibility depends on available traffic, baseline performance, and the smallest effect the test is intended to detect.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://help.amplitude.com/docs/en/feature-experiment/workflow/experiment-estimate-duration :: Estimate the duration of your experiments | Amplitude Docs

required_facts.statement: Use those inputs to estimate sample needs and duration before building or starting the experiment.
source_refs: amplitude_playbook#https://help.amplitude.com/docs/en/feature-experiment/workflow/experiment-estimate-duration :: Estimate the duration of your experiments | Amplitude Docs

misconceptions.statement: Small desired improvements can require more traffic and longer runtimes than larger effects.

briefs.learning_objective: Use data as a primary input to a product decision, while recognizing its limits.
